sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Go's compilation model makes it uniquely well-suited for Docker containers, and interviewers at companies using Go in production will ask about this. The multi-stage build pattern, CGO_ENABLED=0 for static binaries, and the scratch or distroless base image are all specific to Go and show up in fresher interviews at any company deploying Go services. This is also the content that differentiates a fresher who has deployed something from one who has only run `go run main.go`.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
One Go property that drives everything:

- **Go compiles to a single static binary with no runtime dependency.** Unlike Java (needs JVM), Python (needs interpreter + all packages), or Node.js (needs Node runtime + node_modules), a Go binary can run in a container with nothing else — not even a shell. This is why the final Docker image can be as small as a `scratch` image with just the binary.
- **Multi-stage build = build stage + run stage.** The build stage has the Go toolchain (large image, ~800 MB). The run stage is just the binary (potentially <10 MB). The multi-stage pattern is how you get small images without writing complex scripts.
- **`CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build`** — disables C bindings and targets Linux. Produces a fully static binary that runs in a scratch container even if your development machine is macOS.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Dockerfile for Go basics** — `FROM golang:1.22 AS builder`, `COPY go.mod go.sum ./`, `RUN go mod download`, `COPY . .`, `RUN go build -o /app ./cmd/server`
- **Go multi-stage build basics** — second stage: `FROM scratch` or `FROM gcr.io/distroless/static`; `COPY --from=builder /app /app`; `CMD ["/app"]`; result: tiny image with just the binary
- **docker run go binary** — `docker build -t myapp .`; `docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp`; `docker run --rm myapp` to auto-remove container after it stops
- **Environment variables in Docker** — `ENV PORT=8080` in Dockerfile sets a default; `docker run -e PORT=9090 myapp` overrides at runtime; `os.Getenv("PORT")` in Go reads it
- **Docker Compose basics** — `docker-compose.yml` with a `services:` section; `depends_on` for service ordering; `environment:` block for env vars; `ports:` for port mapping; `go` service + `postgres` service is the canonical example

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Why is Go ideal for multi-stage Docker builds?** — The expected answer: Go compiles to a static binary with no runtime dependencies, so the final image only needs the binary itself, not a language runtime. A Go Docker image can be under 10 MB; a comparable Java image is typically 200+ MB.
- **`CGO_ENABLED=0` and why** — by default, some Go packages (like `net` and `os/user`) use CGO to call C libraries. With CGO enabled, the binary is not fully static and requires glibc in the container. `CGO_ENABLED=0` forces pure Go implementations, producing a truly static binary that runs in a scratch container.
- **`scratch` vs `distroless`** — `scratch` is an empty image with only your binary; `distroless/static` adds CA certificates and timezone data, which most services need. Interviewers ask which to choose and why.
- **COPY go.mod go.sum before COPY .** — layer caching. If go.mod and go.sum do not change, Docker reuses the `go mod download` layer. Copying all source first invalidates this cache on every code change.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"For Go Docker images I use a two-stage build. The builder stage uses the official Go image to compile the binary with `CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build`. The final stage uses `FROM gcr.io/distroless/static` and just copies in the binary — no Go toolchain, no shell, nothing else. The result is typically a 10-20 MB image compared to 500 MB for a JVM service. I set `CGO_ENABLED=0` to disable C bindings so the binary is fully static and runs in a scratch or distroless container without glibc."*
